ops.new_text:
The contributions of the study are these:
\begin{itemize}
\item BTTN, a survival network whose ECG evidence passes through per-block frequency and lead factors, with a separate linear clinical term that does not pass through those factors.
\item An incident-AF cohort in MIMIC-IV-ECG defined from ICD-coded hospital diagnoses with a 30-day blanking window, reported with its exclusion counts.
\item A comparison of one-year discrimination against a clinical model, a CNN and linear block-term tensor regression (BTTR) under one protocol, and the discrimination of one survival model at four horizons.
\item The calibration, risk stratification and operating points of BTTN with the clinical term.
\item A beat-aligned, energy-normalised occlusion profile of the ECG term of BTTN.
\end{itemize}

ops.rationale: States the occlusion as carried out in beat_saliency.py lines 33 to 41 at 500 Hz: 12 samples (24 ms), 6 before to 5 after the offset, offsets truncated to a whole sample towards the R peak, so neighbouring windows abut or leave one sample.
ops.new_text: Occlusion sensitivity covers part of the input and records the change in the output \cite{Zeiler_2014}. It is one of the perturbation-based explanation methods \cite{Ivanovs_2021}. We applied it to a single ECG-only BTTN trained on the whole survival sample. For the 120 highest-risk ECGs of patients with an event, a window of 12 samples (24 ms at 500 Hz) was set to zero in every beat of one lead. The window ran from 6 samples before to 5 samples after a fixed offset from each R peak. Each offset was rounded to a whole sample towards the R peak. R peaks were detected on lead II. The spectrogram was rebuilt and the drop in log-risk recorded, for each lead and for offsets from 350 ms before to 425 ms after the R peak in steps of 25 ms. Neighbouring windows abut or leave one sample between them. Zeroing a high-energy part of the beat changes the spectrogram most. Each mean drop was therefore also divided by the mean energy of the removed samples, plus one tenth of that energy's mean over all leads and offsets for stability.

ops.rationale: Names the offsets the five windows group and the offsets that belong to no window (SEG and the centres grid of beat_saliency.py lines 21, 30 and 88 to 91; their energy enters ENG.mean() of line 84), and gives the window width as 24 ms.
ops.new_text: The offsets from 225 ms before to 375 ms after the R peak were grouped into five windows, the P, PR, QRS, ST and T windows. Table~\ref{tab:occlusion} gives the offsets each window contains and the span of the beat that their occlusions cover. The offsets from 350 to 250 ms before the R peak and at 400 and 425 ms after it belong to no window. They are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency}, and their removed energy counts in the mean energy over all leads and offsets that the normalisation adds. They enter no window value. These windows are fixed offsets and are not delineated per beat. A negative mean drop at a lead and offset was set to zero before the window means were taken, for both the raw and the normalised value. The profile of a window is the mean over leads and over the offsets it contains. The replacement value and the window size shape an occlusion map \cite{arxiv_1702_04595}, and the perturbation method and the region size shape the evaluation of attributions on time series \cite{_imi__2025}. The zero replacement and the 24 ms window are therefore choices of this readout. The readout describes the fitted model on its own training ECGs.

ops.new_text: \subsection{Implications of an ECG term built on readable factors, with a separate clinical term}

ops.rationale: Replaces the claim that the factors keep their meaning by the claim Equation 3 supports, and states that the fused model fits its factors beside the clinical term, so they may differ from those of ECG-only BTTN.
ops.new_text: Separating the clinical term from the block-term layer lets the fused model gain discrimination without passing the risk factors through its ECG factors. The ECG evidence still passes through frequency and lead factors, and each risk factor enters the linear term with one weight. The fused model is trained as one network, so its factors are fitted beside the clinical term and may differ from those of ECG-only BTTN. The two sources therefore have separate parameters that can be inspected apart, although this study reports no reading of the fitted frequency and lead factors. In a fused network whose clinical inputs enter the factor layer, the factors could absorb risk-factor information, as concept representations absorb information beyond their concepts \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The architecture of BTTN closes this route for the clinical term. It does not close it for information that the ECG itself carries, which the factors may encode in ways a reader does not expect.

ops.rationale: Gives the PR-window span the occluded samples cover, 136 to 62 ms before the R peak, as in Table 5; the sentence on the mean beat of Figure 3 holds for this span.
ops.new_text: The association is not uniform, and the comparison has a limited scope. In a Swedish cohort of 70-year-olds, the PR interval measured in lead V1 was not related to incident AF, while a short P-wave duration was \cite{Ostrowska_2022}. The cohort studies measure the PR interval from the onset of the P wave to the onset of the QRS complex. The PR window of the readout groups the occlusions centred 125 to 75 ms before the R peak, a fixed span from 136 to 62 ms before it. On the mean beat of Figure~\ref{fig:beat-saliency}, this span holds the end of the P wave and the PR segment. The agreement claimed here therefore concerns the location within the cardiac cycle only. The clinical term holds P-wave duration but no PR interval. One reading of the gain of the fused model is that the ECG term carries information on atrial and atrioventricular conduction that the clinical term does not measure. The present results do not test this reading, which remains a hypothesis.

ops.rationale: The patients with onset after one year are events of the survival design that count as negatives at one year, not controls; the sentence now says so.
ops.new_text: The evaluation of calibration and operating points has limits as well. The probabilities were recalibrated in the evaluation sample with two-fold cross-fitting, so the calibration of the model in another population is not shown. The one-year design sampled four controls per case, and the survival design sampled cases and controls. PPV was therefore recomputed at the proportion of cases among the cases and AF-free controls of the one-year design, 1,855 in 43,625. This proportion exceeds the one-year rate of the survival cohort, 1,855 in 50,545, whose one-year negatives include the patients with onset after one year. The PPVs of Table~\ref{tab:operating} are therefore upper values for that population. The study also reports no table of the characteristics of cases and controls and no count of missing values per clinical factor. The sample therefore cannot be compared with another population on these measures.

ops.rationale: Gives the occlusion width as carried out, 24 ms.
ops.new_text: The occlusion readout is a perturbation explanation of the fitted model on 120 high-risk training ECGs. It is open to the critiques of post-hoc attribution \cite{arxiv_1810_03292,arxiv_1806_10758,Arends_2026}. Its zero replacement, its 24 ms window and its fixed windows relative to the R peak shape the profile, since the replacement value and the window size shape an occlusion map \cite{arxiv_1702_04595}. The perturbation method and the region size likewise shape the evaluation of attributions on time series \cite{_imi__2025}. Another replacement could change the order of the windows. Readable factors do not by themselves show that the nonlinear head routes its decision through them in the way their reading suggests \cite{arxiv_2106_13314}. The readability of BTTN rests on its architecture, and this study reports no measurement of how far the factors carry the decision on ICD-coded labels.
